correctness.rationale: The floor-ceiling identity gives the exact one-step kernel. Geometric holding times give exact pgf and moments. Under n/2^r -> 0, exponential coupling has L1 error O(n/2^r) after scaling. For fixed q, grouping equal ceiling rates into q independent exponential order-statistic maxima yields the precise q-fold Gumbel limit. For diverging q, the Lyapunov third-moment ratio is O(min(q,n)^(-1/2)), proving the normal law. The standalone checker executed 6961 finite exact/numerical tests, not treated as a substitute for proof.

originality.rationale: The published limited-precision stochastic-rounding mechanism and general extinction-time universality are acknowledged. The checked primary texts do not state the joint explicit fine-truncation kernel c_j/2^r, its full geometric hitting-time generating function, or the fixed-integer q Gumbel-average versus diverging-q normal classification for scalar fixed-point descent. The new implication requires an arithmetic state-by-state reduction, grouping of q identical exponential rates, and uniform Lyapunov control. Unindexed prior specializations remain a priority risk.
residual_risks: Unindexed prior quantized Markov-chain absorption calculations may derive the same repeated-rate family.
General extinction-time frameworks can yield some limit categories once exact transition rates are independently supplied; the claim does not seek exclusivity for Gaussian or Gumbel methods.
The result depends on downward fine-grid truncation; other finite-bit rounding conventions need a separate analysis.

value.rationale: Finite probability bits and scalar fixed-point descent are a concrete numerical design problem. The exact termination distribution and its q-dependent fluctuation class determine iteration budgets and expose an arithmetic, not merely big-O, consequence of guard-bit quantization. q=1 reproduces classical Gumbel timing; fixed q>1 gives a non-Gumbel average with variance pi^2/(6q); divergent q gives a normal limit. The mathematical object is natural and the precision-sensitive distribution is not implied by first-moment convergence estimates.
